title: Nonlocal Thermoelectric Transport in Degenerate Electron Systems
authors: Albert Beardo, Adrián Ramos-Martín, Jordi Tur-Prats, F. Xavier Alvarez, Juan Camacho
abstract: When the characteristic length scales of transport become comparable to the carrier mean free path, the local constitutive description breaks down. We develop the Flux Derivative Formalism (FDF), a kinetic framework that provides a systematic route from the Boltzmann equation to nonlocal constitutive equations. We use it to derive coupled equations for charge and heat transport in isotropic electronic systems, together with boundary conditions derived consistently within this approach, yielding a closed macroscopic description that can be applied to complex geometries without solving the full Boltzmann problem. The explicit transport coefficients are derived for degenerate electronic systems within the Callaway model. A central result is that varying the relative strength of resistive and momentum-conserving collisions changes the transport coefficients but not the non-local constitutive structure, providing a continuous description from resistive-dominated transport to the collective hydrodynamic limit. The electronic heat equation takes a Guyer-Krumhansl form, whose predictions are validated against size-dependent thermal-transport measurements in Cu and Ni. For coupled thermoelectric transport, the resulting boundary-value problem determines the complete geometry-dependent transport matrix. Comparison with spatially resolved Boltzmann solutions confirms quantitative accuracy down to transverse dimensions comparable to the carrier mean free path. The theory predicts geometry-dependent Seebeck and Peltier coefficients while preserving Onsager reciprocity and the Kelvin relation.
summary: This work develops the Flux Derivative Formalism (FDF) to create a rigorous, nonlocal macroscopic theory for thermoelectric transport in degenerate electron systems. By extending the Boltzmann equation, the authors derive coupled constitutive equations that remain valid even when transport lengths are comparable to the electron mean free path. This provides a powerful, geometry-dependent tool for modeling heat and charge flow in complex nanoscale devices.
main_problem: The paper addresses the breakdown of local constitutive descriptions for thermoelectric transport when characteristic length scales approach the carrier mean free path.
main_result: They derive a closed, macroscopic, nonlocal description for coupled charge and heat transport, predicting geometry-dependent transport coefficients while preserving fundamental thermodynamic relations.
method: The core methodology is the Flux Derivative Formalism (FDF), a kinetic framework used to systematically derive nonlocal constitutive equations from the Boltzmann transport equation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on degenerate electron systems (metals) undergoing coupled charge and heat transport, using the Callaway model for collision physics.
key_observables: Geometry-dependent Seebeck and Peltier coefficients, the full geometry-dependent transport matrix, and the electronic heat equation taking a Guyer-Krumhansl form.
important_parameters: The ratio of transport length scales to the carrier mean free path, and the relative strength of resistive versus momentum-conserving collisions.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the non-equilibrium distribution function can be systematically expanded in terms of spatial and temporal derivatives of the transport fluxes, and that the system is degenerate.
figures_summary: Figure 7 benchmarks the normalized Seebeck coefficient comparison between the FDF and BTE methods for linear and parabolic dispersions in 2D and 3D geometries.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the need for nonlocal treatment, details the FDF methodology by expanding the distribution function, and applies this framework to derive coupled equations for charge and heat transport, concluding with comparisons to established Boltzmann solutions.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state transport, the development of a systematic kinetic closure (FDF) to handle non-equilibrium dynamics over finite length scales is a general theoretical tool applicable to open quantum systems where spatial gradients are crucial.

FIG. 2. Closure of electrical counterflows j(r) under a thermal gradient in an open-circuit strip. Electrical-current stream- lines obtained from the finite-geometry coupled FDF for a two-dimensional (d = 2) parabolic band (z = 2), with r = τC/τR = 1 and W = vF τC. For an electron-like Seebeck response (S0 < 0), with the hot end on the left, the electri- cal current flows toward the cold end at the strip center and returns toward the hot end near the walls. These oppositely directed currents close through transverse currents near the electrically insulating ends. Only the hot end of the strip is shown; the closure near the cold end is equivalent.

FIG. 3. Differential Seebeck effect in wires made of the same metal. (Left) When both branches are thick, their effective Seebeck coefficients are identical and the measured electro- motive force vanishes. (Right) When one branch has a trans- verse size comparable to the kinetic lengths while the other remains thick, their finite-size Seebeck coefficients differ and a nonzero differential voltage is generated. The thick branch provides an internal bulk reference, so that the common bulk thermopower cancels.

FIG. 4. Differential Peltier effect in wires made of the same metal. (a, top) When both wires are thick, their Peltier co- efficients are identical and no net Peltier heat is exchanged with the environment at the junction, QP = 0. (a, bottom) When one wire has a transverse size comparable to ℓC while the other remains thick, their finite-width Peltier coefficients differ and a nonzero Peltier heat QP = I(Πthin −Πthick) is absorbed or released at the junction. (b) A possible configu- ration in which the corresponding heating and cooling gener- ate a temperature difference across an electrically insulating sample S.

FIG. 5. Finite-width Seebeck response used as a kinetic benchmark of the FDF for a two-dimensional strip of thickness W. Curves are the complete coupled FDF predictions and symbols are spatially resolved BTE results as the relative strength of momentum-conserving and resistive scattering is varied through τR/τC = 1/r. Left: linear dispersion (z = 1). Right: parabolic dispersion (z = 2); the FDF curves and BTE symbols for the different values of r overlap. The agreement improves systematically with increasing W/(vF τC). The strip is used as a controlled benchmark of the constitutive closure, not as a privileged experimental geometry.
